newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-British Airways profits hit new high.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-British Airways profits hit new high.

text.p: British Airways announced record profits and a bumper share-out for staff on Monday, thanks to continued strong growth in air markets worldwide, but warned that the strength of the pound could hit results in the current year.

"Sterling's current strength will adversely impact profits although it is anticipated that this will at least partially be offset by lower fuel prices and further business efficiency improvement," chairman Sir Colin Marshall said in his results statement.

Pre-tax profits rose 9.4 percent to 640 million pounds for the year to March 31, which BA said was achieved despite a surprise jump in oil prices pushing up the fuel bill by 20 percent to 842 million pounds.

The final dividend was increased by a penny to 10.8 pence a share, to take the total payout for the year to 15.05 pence, up 10.3 percent, while BA's 58,210 staff are to share 89 millon pounds of profits under a bonus scheme.
The formerly state-owned airline also announced it was giving every employee 10 shares apiece to celebrate its tenth anniversary in the private sector.
But the share price fell 18-1/2 pence to 741-1/2p after the results.
The company also made an exceptional charge of 127 million pounds to cover restructuring costs associated with its "Business Efficiency" programme.
This was offset in the headline result by an exceptional gain of 125 million pounds which BA made by reversing a 50 percent writeoff made on its investment in former partner US Airways two years ago.
BA said it was restoring the value of its original $400 million investment in the airline in preparation for the planned sale of its stake.

Chief executive Robert Ayling declined to say when the sale might go ahead, however. BA announced in December it planned to sell the 24.6 percent shareholding following its move to team up with US Airways' bigger rival, American Airlines.
Ayling also declined to say when he expected to see any movement in the long-running approvals process for the tie-up with American, which had been interrupted by the British election.
The new Labour government has the task of reviewing the deal in tandem with investigations by the European Union (EU) and the U.S. government.

"I don't expect to hear by any specific date but I think that the momentum is building up again," Ayling told Reuters. "There was inevitably a delay during the period of the election and the authorities here and in Washington and the (EU) Commission in Brussels are all now working again on the case.
"It's a very important deal for us and we are not putting a gun to anyone's head with a particular timetable....We are prepared to be patient about this."
Ayling also said it was too early to predict whether the strength of sterling would be fully offset by other factors in this year's results.
"Clearly currency is an important factor and if it (sterling) stays at its current levels it will make an impact but we believe there are a lot of other offsetting features," he said.
The company said the unexpected jump in oil prices added 142 million pounds to its fuel costs last year, and led to a fall of 55 million pounds in operating profits.
"We have produced very good results this year and absorbed 142 million pounds worth of additional fuel prices," Ayling said.
"But we have a duty to point out to the markets that the current price of sterling is something which is more than we had expected when we were beginning to plan this year."
Normally the airline reckons that currency fluctuations smooth out over time as it affects foreign currency-denominated costs as well as ticket sales.

Meanwhile the company was progressing with its "business efficiency" campaign programme, aimed at finding a billion pounds of savings in annual costs by March 2000 from outsourcing and rationalisation of all parts of the business. BA said that action taken in the last year meant it had already found 600 million pounds of the target. But Ayling warned that it would not be easy to find the remaining 400 million pounds.
"We have got a long way to go and I don't want people to feel that this is going to be easy," he told Reuters.

Initiatives announced so far include pay and job restructuring deals in baggage handling and the World Cargo division, rationalisation of some accounting functions, closure of its loss-making Contract Handling business serving third-party airline traffic at London Heathrow and outsourcing of ground vehicles services and catering operations.
